thread.title: Charting a post-election downdraft, S&P 500 returns to mini-crash range

author: Michael Ashbaugh
title: Charting a post-election downdraft, S&P 500 returns to mini-crash range
text:
Editor’s Note: This is a free edition of The Technical Indicator, a daily MarketWatch subscriber newsletter. To get this column each market day, click here.
Technically speaking, the U.S. benchmarks’ fleeting post-election rally attempt has fizzled.
In the process, the S&P 500 has violated notable support — including the 200-day moving average — selling off respectably to the former October range from well-defined resistance.
Before detailing the U.S. markets’ wider view, the S&P 500’s SPX, +0.21% hourly chart highlights the past two weeks.
As illustrated, the S&P has extended its pullback from the range top (2,817).
In the process, the index has violated its 200-day moving average, currently 2,762, a widely-tracked longer-term trending indicator. Though traversing less-charted territory, deeper support (2,710) matches the March gap.
Meanwhile, the Dow Jones Industrial Average has pulled in from one-month highs.
Tactically, the June peak (25,402) remains an inflection point, and is followed by the deeper 200-day moving average, currently 25,104.
This is the lone widely-tracked U.S. benchmark positioned atop its 200-day.
True to recent form, the Nasdaq Composite’s backdrop remains the weakest of the big three U.S. benchmarks.
Recall that major resistance spans from 7,474 to the 200-day moving average, currently 7,517.
Friday’s session high (7,474) matched resistance, and the Nasdaq has followed through aggressively lower, dropping as much as 5% from the November peak.
Tactically, the breakdown point (7,274) closely matches gap resistance.
Widening the view to six months adds perspective.
On this wider view, the Nasdaq has gapped back under its 200-day moving average and the 7,474 resistance.
The downturn punctuates a “lower high” at the November peak versus the mid-October peak, consistent with an intermediate-term downtrend, to the extent the benchmarks are currently “trending.”
Delving deeper, the 2017 peak (7,004) marks an inflection point, and is followed by the October low (6,922).
Looking elsewhere, the Dow Jones Industrial Average remains the strongest widely-tracked U.S. benchmark.
Still, Monday’s 602-point plunge punctuated a violation of the 50-day moving average, currently 25,848. The downturn filled the November gap.
To reiterate, the June peak remains an inflection point (25,402) and is followed by the deeper 200-day moving average.
Meanwhile, the S&P 500 has failed its initial retest of the range top (2,817), reversing firmly under the 200-day moving average.
Tactically, the May peak (2,742) remains an inflection point and is followed by the deeper 2,710 support.
The bigger picture Broadly speaking, the late-year price action remains jagged and the prevailing backdrop is not one-size-fits-all.
On a headline basis, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite have violated major support, including the marquee 200-day moving average.
Meanwhile, the Dow industrials remain relatively resilient — to use the term loosely — retaining a posture atop the 200-day moving average. (The Dow also briefly spiked atop the mid-October peak, outpacing the other benchmarks.)
But as always, the Dow industrials is a price-weighted index, with just 30 components, making it the least representative broad-market gauge.
Moving to the small-caps, the iShares Russell 2000 ETF’s backdrop IWM, +0.31% remains incrementally weaker.
As detailed repeatedly, the November rally attempt has been fueled by decreased volume against the backdrop of a pending death cross. (A bearish 50-day/200-day moving average crossover is more succinctly known as a death cross, and in this case, will likely signal Wednesday.)
To be sure, the crossover is frequently a lagging indicator, though it exemplifies the extensive late-year technical damage. The small-caps’ prevailing backdrop remains firmly bearish pending repairs.
Similarly, the SPDR S&P MidCap 400’s November rally attempt has lacked follow-through.
In its case, the bearish 50-day/200-day moving average crossover has signaled early Tuesday, indicating that the intermediate-term downtrend has overtaken the longer-term trend.
Looking elsewhere, the SPDR Trust S&P 500 SPY, +0.15% has nailed its range top (281.15), topping within seven cents across consecutive sessions.
The SPY has subsequently violated notable support.
Tactically, notable overhead spans from 275.30 to 275.90, an area matching gap resistance and the 200-day moving average. A sustained break higher would mark technical progress.
Against this backdrop, the S&P 500’s fleeting post-election spike has also fizzled.
Consider that the S&P nailed its range top last week — topping just under resistance (2,817) — and has reversed aggressively, violating several support points, including the 200-day moving average.
Amid the downturn, Monday’s market breadth statistics registered as firmly negative. Declining volume surpassed advancing volume by a nearly 5-to-1 margin on the NYSE and the Nasdaq, signaling that bearish momentum remains in play.
So collectively, establishing a durable market low will likely be a process, not an event. The bottoming process may be underway — time will tell — though the S&P 500’s intermediate- to longer-term technical bias remains bearish pending repairs. The prevailing risk remains to the downside.
Tactically, the S&P’s 50-day moving average, currently 2,822, is descending toward the range top (2,817). An eventual close higher would mark a “higher high” — also placing it above the mini-crash range — raising the flag to a potentially legitimate rally attempt.
See also: Charting the S&P 500’s November bounce ahead of U.S. midterms.
See also: Cracks surface in the bull trend, S&P 500 nails major support.
Tuesday’s Watch List — Charting three November market headwinds Drilling down further, three headline developments punctuate the prevailing market headwind — Apple’s November downdraft, a surging U.S. dollar and crude oil’s persistent plunge.
To start, Dow 30 component Apple, Inc. AAPL, -0.07% started November with a sharp gap lower, pressured after the company’s third-quarter results, and decision to discontinue reporting unit sales for iPhones.
The subsequent rally attempt has been flat — capped by the breakdown point — and punctuated by an incremental downturn to the 200-day moving average, currently 193.36. Shaky price action.
The 200-day roughly matches the August breakout point, circa 194.20, and a closing violation would raise a technical red flag. Deeper support, circa 182.20, closely matches the June range bottom.
Conversely, notable resistance matches the post-breakdown peak (210.12) and an eventual close higher would place the brakes on bearish momentum.
Meanwhile, the U.S. dollar is trending higher, surging amid rising Treasury yields and a late-year safe-haven trade.
As illustrated, the Invesco U.S. Dollar Bullish ETF has knifed to 19-month highs punctuating a successful test of the breakout point.
Delving slightly deeper, trendline support closely tracks the 50-day moving average, currently 25.40. The dollar’s intermediate- to longer-term bias remains firmly bullish barring a violation.
Finally, the United States Oil Fund USO, -5.13% has asserted a persistent late-year downtrend. The fund tracks the price of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) light, sweet crude oil.
Consider that the shares have plunged as much as 23% from the October peak, and are vying Tuesday for the longest losing streak on record.
Technically, the downtrend is powerful, violating all kinds of support, including the 200-day moving average to start November.
Tactically, initial resistance matches the breakdown point (13.00) and is followed by the 200-day moving average, an area matching trendline resistance. An eventual close atop the trendline would mark a step toward stabilization.
